nodes.question: What does "NCP" stand for in the context of this paragraph?
nodes.answer: NCP stands for nature's contribution to people.
nodes.paragraph: Measures of these strategies, programs and policies follow different conservation concepts (see B scher and Fletcher 2020 ) and include (i) the protection of areas, habitats and species, (ii) active support of biodiversity (e.g. less intensive land- and sea use, environmental schemes,promotion of green infrastructure, restoration of habitats and ecosystems, reduction of introduction of non-native or invasive species, conservation action for threatened spe-cies), as well as (iii) using biodiversity sustainably (e.g. related to sheries, forestry). Despite major efforts, the ongoing loss of biodiversity at global, regional and locallevels and its various consequences for ecosystem func- tions, nature S contribution to people (NCP) and human well-being, has hardly been mitigated. Indeed, despite someprogress, most global and European biodiversity targets have been missed or only partly achieved (IPBES 2018 , 2019 ; European Environment Agency 2020 ,2024; Secre- tariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity 2020 ; P rtner et al. 2021 ; Biermann et al. 2022 ; Perino et al. 2022 ).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Sustainable water resource management|Nature-based solutions_qna_001
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What methodology was developed and applied in this study to prioritize Nature-based Solutions and Bioeconomy Solutions?
nodes.answer: A participatory, cross-sectoral multi-criteria assessment (MCA) decision-support tool was developed and applied.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Climate change challenges necessitate innovative, effective and sustainable mitigation measures to enhance ecosystem resilience. This study presents the development and ap - plication of a participatory, and cross-sectoral multi-criteria assessment (MCA) decision- support tool designed to prioritize Nature-based Solutions (NBS) and Bioeconomy Solu - tions (BES) based on Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem (WEFE) nexus and selected impact (Social, Economic, Climate change, Institutional) criteria. The methodology and tool are adaptable in different contexts and can address several climate change, sustainability, and circularity challenges. The participatory MCA methodology was applied and validated during an all-day workshop on Tinos, a Greek island on the Aegean Sea. Local challenges were addressed and examined within the framework of two distinct sites. Workshop results identified habitat loss and biodiversity decline as the island S primary challenges, with Conservation Agriculture and Agroforestry emerging as the top-rated solutions, scoring 78/100 and 71/100, respectively. Although stakeholders prioritized different interventions for each site, the selected solutions consistently aimed to address these environmental issues. This research study contributes to advancing understanding and practice in the field of sustainable resource management within the WEFE nexus, while underscoring the importance of participatory approaches in developing effective and context-specific sustainability strategies.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Sustainable water resource management|Nature-based solutions_qna_002
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What solutions are suggested to address the effects of climate change in the Mediterranean region?
nodes.answer: The suggested solutions include the implementation of Nature-based Solutions (NBS) and Bioeconomy Solutions (BES) that focus on utilizing local natural resources and biowaste.
nodes.paragraph: Keywords Nature-based Solutions Bioeconomy WEFE nexus Multi-criteria Assessment Participatory Workshop et al. [full author details at the end of the article] 1 3 Circular Economy and SustainabilityIntroduction During the last decades, the Mediterranean basin has faced increased environmental chal - lenges related to climate change and increased urbanization [ 1]. Extensive droughts dur - ing summer have aggravated the desertification of the region [ 2] which, coupled with the subsequent wildfires and increased floodings, has put pressure on its natural resources. Cli - mate change effects ought to be addressed by adopting better practices for managing vital resources, such as water, energy, and food, as well as recognizing their interconnections. Based on the latter, in the last years, scientists, researchers, and policymakers have explored the Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem nexus approach which emphasizes the interac - tions between those sectors and promotes integrated strategies [ 3, 4]. Strategies that deal with the effects of climate change while covering the WEFE nexus include the implemen - tation of Nature-based Solutions (NBS) [ 5, 6], and Bioeconomy Solutions (BES), which emphasize the importance of local natural resources and biowaste as part of the solution.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Sustainable water resource management|Nature-based solutions_qna_004
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What do NBS approaches prioritize in their application?
nodes.answer: NBS approaches prioritize the conservation and restoration of natural systems as well as the creation of novel ecosystems to address societal and environmental challenges.
nodes.paragraph: NBS and BES are related concepts, but they have distinct applications, objectives, and priorities. NBS refer to approaches that use nature or natural processes to address social and environmental challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and water scarcity [ 7 9]. NBS prioritize the conservation and restoration of natural systems as well as the creation of novel ecosystems to address societal and environmental challenges [ 10]. On the other hand, BES focus on using biological resources to create economic value and reduce envi - ronmental impact [ 11]. Bioeconomy offers an alternative not only to waste minimization and circular economy but also to efficient natural resource management and the increase of food security. In particular, sustainable bioresources (from agricultural, marine, plant wastes, etc.) can be used for the production of biogas, biochar, bio-chemicals, and other by-products, which in turn can be used for further production processes, such as bio-energy, fuels, and fertilizers, or as mediums for purification and decontamination of wastewater [12]. Separately or combined, NBS and BES are well-suited approaches for applying the Water-Food-Energy-Ecosystems (WEFE) nexus perspective to human activities.

nodes.question: In what way can NBS and BES be applied together?
nodes.answer: NBS and BES can be applied separately or combined to effectively approach the Water-Food-Energy-Ecosystems (WEFE) nexus perspective in human activities.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Sustainable water resource management|Nature-based solutions_qna_006
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: In what contexts has MCA been widely applied?
nodes.answer: MCA has been widely applied in nature-based solutions (NBS) and built environment solutions (BES) in engineering, natural resources management, and climate adaptation and resilience.
nodes.paragraph: Although the WEFE nexus approach is widely accepted in research and science, imple - menting WEFE nexus solutions at the local scale requires acceptance from the local com - munity, as well as community-based insights and knowledge [ 13]. Participatory approaches, where stakeholders from the local environment actively participate in co-shaping the parameters and importance of implementation strategies, are therefore of high significance [14 16]. As such, decision methods like the Multi-Criteria Assessment (MCA), are suitable for facilitating informative stakeholder interactions for the prioritization of key attributes of the system, or its overall evaluation. Through MCA processes, stakeholder engagement and participation can promote informed and relevant decision-making and enhance the applica - bility and acceptance of the decisions. However, it should be noted that MCA methodolo - gies face some limitations, such as subjectivity in assigning weights, oversimplification of trade-offs, and challenges in integrating conflicting stakeholder perspectives [ 17, 18]. MCA has been widely applied in NBS and BES applications in engineering, in natural resources management and climate adaptation and resilience. It has been used to address themes such as flood risk management, ecosystem services, and environmental sustain - ability on different scales.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Sustainable water resource management|Nature-based solutions_qna_007
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How does the presented methodology enable the evaluation and selection of NBS/BES solutions?
nodes.answer: The methodology utilizes a participatory MCA approach to evaluate, compare, select, and prioritize NBS/BES solutions that integrate the elements of the WEFE nexus.
nodes.paragraph: The innovative aspects of this work lie in the development of a participatory MCA methodology that combines both NBS and BES with the four elements of the WEFE nexus and additional criteria related to social, climatic, insti - tutional and economic aspects, and the development of a web-based MCA decision-making tool to be used during multi-stakeholder workshops. To the best of our knowledge, similar methodologies have not been developed or applied in the context of Greece. Methodology The methodological process behind this work regards (Fig. 1) (i) the development of a tool based on a participatory MCA approach, which enables it to evaluate, compare, select, and prioritize NBS/BES solutions that integrate the WEFE nexus (Sect. 2.1), (ii) the customiza - tion and replicability of the NBS/BES tool, which allows its adaptability and replicability in various contexts (Sect. 2.2) and (iii) the steps for the application of the NBS/BES tool at in-person workshops (Sect. 2.3). Two case studies on Tinos Island in Greece are presented to demonstrate the customization and application of the tool.
